items.summary: NANOROBOT-ENHANCED DIGITAL TWINS OF BRAIN STATE AT THE LIMIT A multiscale, uncertainty-aware research atlas on microrobotic observations, neural inverse problems, active model discrimination and the limits of computational brain twins. This research monograph asks whether additional microscale observations or strictly bounded reversible experiments can distinguish competing neural-state models that explain conventional measurements equally well. The twin is explicitly defined as a versioned scientific belief, not a digital person, a mind reader or a clinically validated instrument. Its objective is not maximum model complexity but improved identifiability, calibrated prediction under new conditions and faithful retention of failed hypotheses. The work develops five layers: multiscale neural and microenvironment state representation; posterior equivalence and prior sensitivity; non-clinical safe experimental design; frozen-version forking, rollback and reference ancestry; and blind prospective validation against classical state-space systems and independently specified alternatives. Its research architecture includes 30 distinct mathematical derivation plates linked to later chapters, 82 chapters with five independently paginated research sections apiece, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 revisable Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger identifies existing support for brain modeling, latent neural dynamics, experiment design and preclinical microrobot tracking while preventing those sources from being mistaken for evidence of the proposed integrated system. Key research questions include: Can two equally accurate virtual brains be separated by a small, permissible observation? How can the effect of a measurement itself be separated from neural change? When does a prior dominate the inferred brain state? Can the model predict unseen function rather than reconstruct a training signal? Can another laboratory reproduce a rejected twin and safely return to an earlier version? SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This is a forward-looking, non-clinical research synthesis and experimental hypothesis architecture. It provides no personal medical advice, patient-specific interpretations or instruction to deliver neural interventions. Existing murine microrobot tracking and virtual-brain modeling studies do not establish autonomous neural nanorobot readout, human safety, privacy-sensitive mind inference or therapeutic efficacy. Proposed formulas, experiments, research gates and answer embryos are not newly validated biological laws or executed experiments. The work keeps independent safety vetoes, privacy, external reproducibility and explicit model retirement as first-class constraints. Research questions remain open to refutation, correction and reconstruction by future human and AI researchers.

items.summary: We study the relation between equal-weight circle quadrature, Gauss--Chebyshev quadrature, and planar Minkowski reconstruction. The regular $N$-point grid is an $\mathbb S^1$-design of strength $N-1$; a half-step rotation of the $2M$-point grid projects to the classical $M$-point Gauss--Chebyshev rule. A common family of quadrature-error functionals gives exact identities for integration error, mixed-area error, and support-function error. For $N\ge3$, the centered Minkowski polygon $P_N$ with perimeter $2π$ has the exact Hausdorff distance from the unit disk $B^2$ \[ d_H(P_N,B^2)=1-\fracπ{N}\cot\fracπ{N} =\frac{π^2}{3N^2}+O(N^{-4}). \] With Steiner centering, we obtain $d_H(K_μ,K_ν)\leπW_1(μ,ν)$ for balanced, nondegenerate probability measures, where $W_1$ uses geodesic distance. Its exponent is sharp even for smooth positive densities near the uniform measure. The identity $W_1(ν_N,σ)=π/(2N)$ yields a general $O(N^{-1})$ bound for the regular grid. The sharper $O(N^{-2})$ rate follows from the sparse discrepancy spectrum and the inverse multiplier $(1-k^2)^{-1}$. Finally, a perturbation estimate gives sufficient conditions for preserving the quadratic rate and its leading constant.
items.title: Gauss--Chebyshev Quadrature, $\mathbb S^1$-Designs, and the Planar Minkowski Inverse Problem: A One-Dimensional Model for Design-Induced Convex Geometry

items.summary: World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions. We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes. We see the following benefits: 1) Alignment: linear probes read robot and object state from LeWAM's latent better than from a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while the latent ignores visual distractors as well as LeWM does and far better than a reconstruction-based WAM. 2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match a regular flow-matching policy trained on the same encoder at matched size, while also providing a world model. 3) Planning: Sampling raw actions when planning with WAMs lets MPC exploit dynamics-model inaccuracies; planning in the noise space of the policy head instead improves the closed-loop performance of these WAMs.
items.title: LeWAM: A JEPA World Action Model with Diffusion-Steering-Based MPC

items.summary: Solutions to geophysical inverse problems are generally non-unique, and greatly benefit from additional geological prior information. Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are commonly used to parametrise such information, typically restricting solutions to a lower-dimensional latent space. The final inversion result is obtained by mapping the latent space parameters to the original higher-dimensional model space using the GNNs. However, solutions then remain confined to a low-dimensional geological generative manifold; if the true Earth model lies outside of this manifold, standard latent space inversion fails. We propose a Bayesian model space inversion method that uses the generative manifold as a guide to find the solutions that lie outside this manifold. We validate our approach in non-linear travel-time tomography experiments on both simple and more geological structures. By comparing our method with model space inversion using uniform prior probabilities and standard latent-space inversion, we demonstrate that the less informative uniform prior fails to constrain the solution, while the latent space approach fails when the true Earth model lies outside of the generative manifold. Conversely, our new model-space inversion method successfully recovers complex off-manifold geological features while maintaining low solution uncertainty.
items.title: Escaping Geological Generative Prior Distributions in Bayesian Travel Time Tomography

items.summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.
items.title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition

items.summary: This technical note documents a conditional mathematical correspondence between the static spatial kernel used in conventional electromagnetic potential theory and the fixed-source gravitational potential in Lisa Doumbouya’s Harmonic Physics programme. Under supplied three-dimensional Euclidean geometry, spherical symmetry and stated boundary conditions, the derivation gives the static Green function 1/(4πr). Applying the existing gravitational source normalization yields the potential −μ/r, whose radial derivative gives the inward acceleration −μ/r². The note distinguishes potential, field amplitude, intensity, acceleration and optical measurement conversion, keeping geometric normalization separate from the distance exponent. The optical phase-ruler results are reviewed alongside the GRACE-FO forward forecasts. Calibrated reconstruction using measured phase retained micrometre-scale agreement with processed microwave ranging, while some forward models produced much larger errors. These results do not establish exponential error growth or identify a unique physical cause. The correspondence uses established mathematics and remains conditional on the supplied geometry, source calibration and physical interpretation. It does not establish an electromagnetic mechanism of gravity or derive spatial geometry from foundational Phase. The note includes the analytical proof, assumptions, evidence boundaries and requirements for a subsequent physical test. No new experimental data are introduced.
items.title: Inverse Radius Kernel and Optical Phase Registration

items.summary: This paper develops a new predefined-time integral reinforcement learning framework for optimal control of unknown nonlinear systems. The unknown drift is first approximated by a radial basis function (RBF) neural network, together with a data-driven online identification law for updating the corresponding neural weights. After the identifier converges to a sufficiently small neighborhood of the true dynamics, the learned model is incorporated into the integral reinforcement learning (IRL) problem. Unlike conventional reinforcement-learning-based optimal control, the desired convergence time is introduced directly into the control objective: a Lyapunov function and its prescribed decay behavior are specified by the designer, and inverse-optimal control is then used to construct a compatible running cost whose optimal policy inherits the predefined-time stabilization property. The value function is approximated by a second RBF neural network, and a new critic update law is developed to impose predefined-time convergence on the critic weights. Finite informative learning data are stored in a replay buffer and reused during the critic update, thereby avoiding the need for persistent excitation throughout the closed-loop operation. Theoretical analysis proves that the critic-weight error enters a prescribed residual set within the allocated learning horizon, while the closed-loop state reaches a small neighborhood of the origin within the overall designer-specified deadline. Numerical simulations on an unknown nonlinear system verify accurate drift reconstruction, predefined-time critic learning, and closed-loop convergence.
items.title: Predefined-Time Integral Reinforcement Learning for Unknown Nonlinear Systems via Inverse-Optimal Design

items.summary: Fisher information metric tensors for the 41 held-out SONICOM test subjects, as used in “Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information” (D. Bassett). Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/domfrbassett/fisher-rao-hrtf-upsampling What the tensors are At each of the 793 directions of the SONICOM grid, the 2×2 tensor g = JᵀΣ⁻¹J describes how well the auditory cues separate that direction from its neighbours. J is the spatial Jacobian of the cues: Barumerli monaural PGE features, ILD and MaxIACCe-transformed ITD, each fitted with real spherical harmonics. Σ holds the cue noise (σ_mon = 1.25 dB, σ_ILD = 1 dB, σ_ITD = 0.569). All fields are low-pass filtered at 16 kHz before the cues are extracted. The tensor is expressed in a local tangent basis u₁ = a × r, u₂ = r × u₁, where a = z, or y when |r_z| > 0.9, and its units are d′² per rad². Contents metric_tensors.zip has one folder per subject, metric_tensors/subject_####/ , containing 25 files per subject (1,025 in total): reference_metric_tensor.mat : the dense measured HRTF. <METHOD>_N###_metric_tensor.mat : one file per reconstruction. There are six methods: SUpDEq_SH , SUpDEq_MCA , SUpDEq_NN_MCA_6dB (SUpDEq-Natural-MCA in the paper), SUpDEq_Bary_MCA_6dB , RANF and FSP_AE . Each is reconstructed from N = 100, 19, 5 and 3 retained directions. The 164 natural-neighbour and barycentric files at N = 5 and 3 have status “ not_applicable ”. The interpolation is undefined for those masks, so these files carry no tensors. Variables in each file: metricTensor : the tensors at SH order 6 [2×2×793]. familyGram : per-cue-family Gram matrices JᵀJ before noise weighting, at SH orders 4, 6 and 8 [2×2×793×3 families×3 orders]. They let you recompute the tensors with other noise values or SH orders. In reconstruction files only: crossFamilyGram : the unsymmetrised cross terms J_refᵀ J_recon, same layout as familyGram . airmByDirection : the pointwise AIRM discrepancy from the reference. Metadata: coordinates (Cartesian and azimuth/elevation in degrees), cue band, noise values (reference files only), status (“ completed ” or “ not_applicable ”) and, for not-applicable files, a message giving the reason. SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.
items.title: Fisher information metric tensors for 'Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information'

items.summary: We establish the overarching mathematical physics framework underlying gravitational screening and electroweak mixing in Big Boot Gauge Theory (BBGT). To demonstrate that the transition from the bare gravitational constant G_bare = 6.514085763e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 (derived from CODATA 2022 constants under unit space-time momentum p = mc = 1 kg m s^-1) to the observed value G_obs = 6.67430e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 is a rigorous topological necessity rather than an arbitrary post-hoc adjustment, we formulate the screening dynamics using Möbius inversion on finite posets over the subgroup lattice of Poincaré Dodecahedral Space (S^3/I^*). We prove that non-associative transit across the e_4 Pati-Salam midpoint node acts as a Möbius topological twist, fixing the geometric inverse-square screening factor S_ZIP^-2 = (1 - 1/120)^-2 = 1.016877348. Combining this with longitudinal Z-leakage (delta_Z = 0.026892000) and non-associative midpoint transit corrections (Delta_assoc = 0.000092701) yields the exact screened laboratory constant without arbitrary tuning.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weak mixing angle (sin^2 theta_W = 1/5 + 1/32 = 0.23125) originates from the pentagonal P_5 symmetry order of the dodecahedron combined with a 2^5 chiral energy cascade, agreeing with experiment (0.23122) to within 0.01%. Finally, we present the complete 8x8 Logical Transitive Index Matrix (T_{n->m}), showing how the 10^19 Planck-to-electroweak mass hierarchy is compressed down to a discrete compilation factor of 128.35 across the aethereal boot levels.

items.summary: Code, 2.5-D finite-wavelength forward solver, datasets, trained models and result files reproducing every number in the manuscript "Source-Conditioned Neural Surrogates for Magnetotelluric Response Prediction Under Finite-Wavelength Excitation" (S. Oh). The study makes the magnetotelluric source an explicit input of a neural forward surrogate. A validated 2.5-D scattered-field solver for a source of finite along-strike wavelength generates the training data; a conditional U-Net predicts the electromagnetic fields, from which impedance and tipper are reconstructed; an aliasing ratio quantifies how much of a source perturbation a plane-wave inversion re-images as conductivity; a surrogate-domain recoverability experiment returns a source estimate close to the known synthetic value, while a direct solver re-forward shows that the recovered conductivity and wavenumber are not together a solver-consistent inverse solution; and magnetometer arrays at three geomagnetic latitudes place real settings on the dimensionless axis that the model defines. CONTENTS: README.md, LICENSE, DATA_LICENSE.txt and requirements.txt are attached unpacked. The code archive holds the analysis scripts (top level and mt3d/) and the full solver source (solver/, with the dataset generator, the Jacobian dump, the re-forward program and the unit tests); it is MIT licensed except the third-party Triangle library, which is redistributed verbatim under its own terms. The data archive holds the three datasets (dataset_dense, dataset_freq, dataset40), the trained checkpoints (ckpt/, mt3d/ckpt/), the joint-inversion and layered-earth training data (mt3d/*.npz), the plane-wave Jacobian dump (phase3/), the solver sweeps (phase1_repro/) and the result files next to the scripts that write them, all under CC BY 4.0 (DATA_LICENSE.txt). Figures and figure-drawing scripts are not included; every figure is a direct plot of a listed result file. Comments have been removed from all code written for this study. Not included: the magnetometer-array time series, which are third-party open data (EarthScope/USArray MT through the IRIS/EarthScope Data Management Center; AusLAMP Musgraves/APY through AuScope and Geoscience Australia, CC BY 4.0) and are rebuilt from those sources by the archived fetch and conversion scripts; and the field-station file that supplies the period list of the two control tests of Section S-XVII (available from the author on request).
items.title: Source-Conditioned Residual Learning for Magnetotelluric Responses Under Finite-Wavelength Excitation

items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
items.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition

items.summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.
items.title: PRB-WM: Physics-Regularized Beta World Models for Predictive Link Adaptation on Real Time-Varying Underwater Acoustic Channels

items.summary: AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AND MISSION OBSERVABILITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation Research Flagship 01 | NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli This research atlas asks a difficult engineering question: when low-Reynolds-number microfluidic flows, Brownian orientation noise, boundary adhesion, external field actuation and incomplete sensing all influence a micro/nanorobot, what would justify calling its behavior autonomous navigation rather than externally assisted motion? The volume treats navigation as an auditable, bounded mission instead of an attractive trajectory. It develops a five-layer program spanning stochastic hydrodynamics, instrument and actuation provenance, uncertainty-calibrated belief-state estimation, blinded microfluidic challenges and independent requalification. Thirty linked mathematical stations differentiate physical relations, information-theoretic functionals and proposed navigation utility measures, with assumptions, dimensions and possible falsifiers. Eighty-two research chapters each open with a core mathematical relation, followed by five independent single-page research sections. Two hundred detailed Research Gates describe decisive comparisons, confounding explanations, evidence requirements, failure conditions and successor handoff artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos offer revisionable research prototypes rather than predetermined conclusions. The key comparator is an equal-budget experiment: fixed-field sequences, microscope-assisted manual control, externally tracked predictive control and candidate fused navigation are evaluated under matched total energy, information access, geometry, time, collision limits and recovery obligations. The manuscript emphasizes blind targets, flow reversal, sensor dropouts, wall adhesion, correlated observations, full-system power accounting, censored failures and post-mission retrieval. A mission arriving at its target but leaving an unrecovered device is not counted as a fully closed success. This work is a hypothesis-generating Research Atlas v1.0, not an experimental report or a validated medical technology. External magnetic, acoustic, optical and microscope infrastructure must be disclosed; no in-vivo or clinical competence is inferred from bench-top movement. Foundational DOI-linked literature provides context, not proof of the proposed integrated system. Every major claim is designed to be revised, rejected or reconstructed by a successor team using raw evidence and pre-registered falsification rules. PARENT RESEARCH DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23046134 Original parent: NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE AT THE LIMIT. Parent-chapter lineage: Ch. 06-11 (navigation), 47-51 (estimation/control), 65 and 68 (benchmarking and transfer). The current child manuscript does not yet have an independent DOI; one would be assigned only upon actual repository deposit. Editorial release note: the manuscript prioritizes non-duplicative research content and independent testability over an artificial word-count target. It is suitable as a research architecture for additional scientific review, not a substitute for physical validation.

items.summary: The underwater sound speed distribution directly governs acoustic propagation paths, rendering it critically important for underwater acoustic communication and target localization. Conventional sound speed profile (SSP) prediction methods provide a good way to estimate the underwater sound speed distribution without on-site data measurement, thus breaking through the coverage area constraints of sonar observation equipment and making the model universal in most marine areas. However, underwater sound speed exhibits multi-scale variations, such as diurnal, quarterly, and intermittent fluctuations caused by ocean processes such as internal waves. This makes it difficult for the fixed structure models in existing methods to have good generalization ability for multi-scale sound speed distribution patterns. To tackle this problem, we proposed a lightweight hybrid basis-function empowered Kolmogorov-Arnold network (LHBF-KAN) model for multi-scale sound speed prediction. We aim to construct a multi-branch representation layer in which different basis functions respond to distinct temporal patterns, from slowly varying background trends to rapid fluctuations induced by dynamic ocean processes, allowing the model to naturally accommodate the inherently multi-scale evolution of sound speed at different depths. To prevent the multi-branch structure from increasing model size, a pruning strategy is further introduced to suppress branches with consistently low contribution during training, yielding a compact architecture, suitable for deployment on resource constrained underwater platforms.
items.title: Robust Prediction of Internal Wave-Affected Multi-Scale Sound Speed Distribution Using Lightweight Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Hybrid Basis Functions

items.summary: Companion code for the preprint "Benchmarking Real-Time DETR Detectors for Multibeam Forward-Looking Sonar: DEIMv2, Detector-Specific Test-Time Fusion, and Domain Shift Analysis on UATD" (Preprints 2026, 2026090449, doi:10.20944/preprints202609.0449.v3). Contains the DEIMv2 engine with UATD configs, the TTA/WBF fusion tooling (default --wbf-rule view-dedup; query-level retained as reproduction control), the paired image-level bootstrap CI scripts, the paper's three central results tables as CSV, and unit tests pinning the WBF view-dedup rule and the bootstrap identity property. items.summary: Underwater acoustic target detection and recognition are essential to marine surveillance and intelligent ocean sensing. Despite substantial advances in deep learning, existing systems typically produce binary detection decisions, categorical labels, or scalar confidence scores, offering limited insight into the physical evidence underlying their outputs. Large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to move underwater acoustic sensing toward interpretable, evidence-grounded understanding; however, generic audio encoders struggle to capture the distinctive physical characteristics of underwater acoustics, and physically annotated data are scarce. In this paper, the first of a two-part series, we propose a from-signals-to-evidence framework that integrates physics-aware acoustic encoding with a pretrained LLM, organized around a unified feature-evidence-decision chain with a shared reasoning core. An open input layer accommodates heterogeneous information-raw waveforms, time-frequency representations, environmental and geographic data, and textual physical priors-unifying detection and recognition within a common formulation. In Part I, we instantiate this framework for target recognition through an Underwater Acoustic Physics-aware Transformer (UPT), which tokenizes complementary acoustic representations and learns task-disentangled physical representations through four physics-oriented learning tasks. We develop a physics-parameterized data engine that provides traceable supervision at two levels of granularity and introduce an attribute-level evaluation protocol to assess the physical fidelity of generated descriptions. Experiments on simulated recordings of four vessels demonstrate accurate vessel recognition and reliable estimation of shaft frequency, blade-passing frequency, and machinery-related attributes.
items.title: From Signals to Evidence: Interpretable Underwater Acoustic Target Sensing with Large Language Models - Part I: Framework and Recognition

items.summary: We investigate the rigidity of smooth stationary solutions to the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in ℝⁿ with singularities along a linear subspace Σ ≅ ℝᵏ. Assuming the scale-invariant transverse bound ‖u(x)‖ ≤ C‖x′‖⁻¹, where x′ ∈ ℝᵐ represents the transverse coordinates and m = n − k is the codimension of the singularity, we prove that u ≡ 0 provided m ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ k < m. This result generalizes the recent theorem of Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie (2026), which corresponds to the case k = 1 and n ≥ 5. Our proof relies on a quantitative local regularity theorem showing that the transverse bound implies the removability of the singularity along Σ. The argument combines weak extension across the subspace, approximate Green functions for the adjoint drift operator, a one-sided bound for the total head pressure, and a localized Frehse–Růžička weighted estimate followed by a finite Stokes–Morrey bootstrap. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of the codimension threshold m ≥ 4 by constructing non-trivial counterexamples for m = 1, m = 2, and m = 3 via trivial extensions of Jeffery–Hamel and Landau solutions, together with a new explicit family of non-trivial solutions in the borderline case m = 1. Finally, we discuss the technical obstruction preventing the immediate removal of the condition k < m and propose a conditional rigidity result under additional integrability assumptions.
items.title: RIGIDITY OF STATIONARY NAVIER–STOKES SOLUTIONS WITH TRANSVERSE BOUNDS NEAR HIGHER-CODIMENSIONAL SINGULAR SUBSPACES

items.summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
items.title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

items.summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.
items.title: PRB-WM: Physics-Regularized Beta World Models for Predictive Link Adaptation on Real Time-Varying Underwater Acoustic Channels

items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
items.title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition

items.summary: This record provides the public, non-confidential analytical and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript “When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? A Borehole-Aware Empirical-to-Synthetic Validation Framework for Urban Tunnelling.” The study develops and audits a borehole-aware empirical-to-synthetic framework for evaluating whether adding downhole seismic information provides defensible incremental value in predicting the Ménard pressuremeter modulus under held-out validation. The empirical benchmark comprises 41 support-matched pressuremeter–seismic records across 21 independent boreholes from the Isfahan Metro Line 2 investigation. The framework compares a reference model, a geotechnical/geological-depth baseline, a seismic-only branch, naive multimodal fusion, and a dependence-aware fusion branch using leave-one-borehole-out validation. The public release contains a de-identified 41-record benchmark dataset, final manuscript Figure 1–5 assets, the current Supplementary Material and Supplementary Figure S1, released derived analytical outputs, provenance and reproducibility documentation, reproducibility and repository-audit scripts, computational-environment specifications, and SHA-256 integrity information. The de-identified dataset replaces source borehole identifiers with pseudonymous identifiers and excludes borehole coordinates and other spatially identifying source information. The underlying Isfahan Metro Line 2 geotechnical, geophysical, and pressuremeter source records are controlled by the Isfahan Urban Railway Organization and are not publicly redistributable. Original source workbooks, proprietary project documents, spatially identifying information, and other restricted source-derived materials are intentionally excluded from this public archive. Permission was obtained to use and publish the de-identified, non-confidential data extracted from the project report and the derived analytical information included in this release. The public code component provides scripts for reproducing the released manuscript-level benchmark metrics and verifying the integrity and consistency of the deposited files. These scripts do not contain the restricted original project records or proprietary source-data processing materials. The archive is intended to support transparent audit and reproducibility of the released derived analyses while preserving the access restrictions applying to the underlying project data.
items.title: When Does Seismic–Geotechnical Data Fusion Add Value? — Project 06 Data and Reproducibility Package

items.summary: Semiconductor spin qubits offer a promising route to compact and scalable quantum computers, combining long coherence times in isotopically purified silicon with compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing. Beyond computational speedup, their energy efficiency is an important consideration for future large-scale systems. We evaluate the power and energy requirements of a Loss-DiVincenzo spin-qubit quantum computer by analyzing the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) and benchmarking it against the classical Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). We develop a detailed energy budget, identifying cryogenic cooling as the dominant baseline contribution before quantum error correction (QEC). The comparison between the QFT and the classical FFT reveals that, for any quantum workload operating under a polynomially bounded sampling regime, the crossover in energy consumption occurs at smaller problem sizes than the crossover in execution time. Thus, quantum computing can become energetically competitive before achieving a speedup in execution time. We then incorporate surface-code QEC and analyze the energy costs of QEC cycles, gate synthesis, and decoding. At scale, instrumentation and decoding become dominant contributions, while cryogenic cooling imposes a constraint on scalability. We show that optimizing the control-signal demultiplexing ratio can reduce the overall energy cost by approximately two orders of magnitude. For a system with about one million physical qubits, we estimate a power consumption of approximately 100 kW, at least one order of magnitude below that of today's highest-performance classical computing systems.
items.title: Energetics of Fault-Tolerant Spin-Qubit Quantum Computation

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a comment on a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview and comments at https://prereview.org/reviews/22745390 . Thank you, Evgenii, for the detailed and constructive PREreview. Your comments led us to substantially strengthen both the experimental design and the interpretation of the results. We have now released a revised version of the manuscript that addresses the main points raised in the review. The revision includes: A 30-seed robustness analysis rather than relying on a single simulation seed A correlation sweep for estimator errors from ρ = 0 to 0.8 Regression-fitted and test-set oracle aggregation baselines Shared-noise experiments for the model–collective calibration signal, reported with ROC-AUC and lift Explicit specification of the four-Wave rolling calibration window, software versions, and PCG64 RNG Portfolio scaling to 100 Feature Blocks using an exact binary MILP reference An explicit separation between budget-constrained portfolio selection and ODP's native dependency-aware sequencing role An exact and scaling benchmark for ODP sequencing under prerequisite constraints An explicit competing-interest disclosure A public reproducibility package containing the simulation code, deterministic seeds, generated data, analysis scripts, and validation material. One particularly useful outcome of the revision was that the stronger experiments narrowed some of our original claims. For example, inverse-MSE aggregation performs very strongly when estimator errors are independent, but its advantage collapses under strong shared error. We also found that ODP distance is not the strongest heuristic for budget-constrained portfolio selection, while it performs very differently in its native sequencing role, where ERS/BVS is exactly optimal for the declared objective without dependencies and remains close to the exact optimum under the tested prerequisite constraints. Revised manuscript: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10648 Reproducibility package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23261325 Thank you again for the review. It improved the paper. Competing interests I am a co-author of the manuscript discussed in this PREreview and a contributor to the D-POAF framework evaluated in the study. I am also affiliated with Inovionix, which develops software implementing D-POAF concepts.
items.title: Comment on a PREreview of "Governed Human-AI Prioritization Under Uncertainty: Adaptive Estimation and Dependency-Constrained Portfolio Selection"

items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention

items.summary: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. Leveraging this diagnostic foundation, \method dynamically compiles observable interaction traces into a provenance graph to pinpoint unresolved dependencies, without accessing private agent states. It then evaluates candidate repairs through an empirical gate that weighs expected gains against disruption risks, and executes repairs only when formal local postconditions hold. Extensive evaluations across demanding benchmarks demonstrate that \method boosts task success by up to 12.3 absolute percentage points on SILO-BENCH and 11.1 on TeamBench. Across both backbones, \method maintains strict cost-effectiveness, adding as little as 2.0\% marginal token overhead. Furthermore, on 562 handoff-relevant traces from the MAST benchmark, \method achieves 69.8\% F1 in a single pass, establishing a reliable operational boundary for verifiable coordination repair.
items.title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Code, trained networks and data for the paper “Physics-informed neural networks for maximizing quantum Fisher information in time-dependent many-body systems”. The archive Zenodo_deposit.zip is self-contained. It holds the training method (a counter-diabatic control expanded in Pauli strings, with a learned schedule, propagated with a fourth-order commutator-free Magnus integrator), the trained network and configuration of every reported run, Supplementary Data 1 (source data of every figure and table), Supplementary Data 2 (pulse files), and a script that regenerates the figures, tables and reported numbers and checks them against the deposited values. Instructions are in README.md inside the archive. Version 2.0.6 re-exports the figure PDFs of the archive; the code, trained networks and data are those of version 2.0.5. Version 2.0.5 corrects the description of the QFI floor and of the stored candidates in the README so that it matches the code, redraws Supplementary Fig. 1 with a key grouped by kind of control, and adds the panels of the time-resolved QFI to Supplementary Fig. 4; the trained networks and data are those of version 2.0.4. Version 2.0.4 completes the regeneration path of the Supplementary Information: python reproduce.py baselines covers every size computed in the paper (ideal control up to twelve qubits), python reproduce.py symmetry also reports the symmetry fractions and compares the Holm-corrected p-values and partial correlations, python reproduce.py verify --exact repeats the dense validation, python reproduce.py replay retrains a paper run against its stored history, and the three runs of the propagation-cadence calibration are included (983 runs). The README documents the selection rules and step control as implemented. Supplementary Data 1 no longer lists the unreported right-limit probe rows of exact_controls.csv ; the trained networks and all other data are unchanged. Download: the archive is stored in eleven parts. Rejoin them with cat Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-* > Zenodo_deposit.zip (on Windows, copy /b Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-aa + Zenodo_deposit.zip.part-ab + ... Zenodo_deposit.zip , listing the parts in order) and check the result with shasum -a 256 -c Zenodo_deposit.zip.sha256 . License: the code is released under the MIT License, and the data, trained networks, figures and tables under CC BY 4.0. Preprint of the first version of the manuscript: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18506
items.title: Physics-informed neural networks for maximizing quantum Fisher information in time-dependent many-body systems

items.summary: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder's final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification.
items.title: LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation

items.summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.
items.title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition

items.summary: Level-2 (restricted) archive, version 1.0.1, of the replication package of the article Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits (H. Jeong, Hanyang University ERICA; manuscript under review). The public Level-1 archive with the programs, tests and aggregate results is https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23226958 (all versions; version 1.0.3, cited in the manuscript: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23430269). Changes in 1.0.1: two files with the per-identity counts of the exploratory published-measure analysis (file-based churn, cohort B; Supplementary Section S13 of the article) were added, re-keyed like the other cohort-B files; every file of version 1.0.0 is unchanged. The files are per-unit derived counts of the 3,687 cohort-A accounts and the cohort-B identities, with random identifiers (marker dates reduced to the month; no account names, e-mail addresses, repository names, commit SHAs or commit times). Placed by python3 reproduce.py --level2 <folder> of the Level-1 package (version 1.0.3), they recompute the registered aggregates and the exploratory aggregates that do not require the raw commit logs, including rates, transitions, paired contrasts, random-exclusion benchmarks and bootstrap intervals; on Python 3.10.12 with numpy 2.2.6 (Linux, aarch64) and on Python 3.13.16 with numpy 2.5.3 (Linux, x86_64) every regenerated result agreed with the reported one (numerical values within 1e-9, text files identical apart from line endings). Access is restricted because cohort-B rows keep the positions of their repositories in the public sampling order, which the registered repository-cluster bootstrap needs. Access is granted to researchers who state their name, affiliation and purpose and who agree to use the files only to verify, reproduce or extend the analyses of the article, not to redistribute the files or per-unit derivatives, not to attempt any re-identification or linkage to public commit histories or accounts, to store the files securely and delete them when the work is complete, and to cite the article and both archives (ACCESS.md). Reviewers of the article receive an access link through the editor.
items.title: Replication package (Level 2, restricted) for "Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits"

items.summary: This repository contains the curated research inputs, analysis code, and reference outputs supporting the study “Supplier identity can reverse estimates of global irrigation savings.” The study examines whether estimates of global irrigation savings depend on which suppliers reduce production, even when displacement quantities are held fixed within each market. It combines crop production, trade, and water-use data with constrained allocation models, historical production-contraction benchmarks, alternative water accounts, and conditional future scenarios for 2050 and 2100. Repository contents 01_Research_Inputs.xlsx — Curated source observations, geographic and crop identifiers, variable definitions, and source citations. 02_Research_Data.sqlite — Larger input datasets, archived analytical outputs, numerical checks, optional derived checkpoints, and an index linking the release to the associated manuscript and supplementary material. Source inputs and computed outputs are explicitly distinguished. 03_Analysis.py — Consolidated Python code containing the analytical modules, dependency specifications, input verification, and reproduction workflow. 04_Readme.txt — Documentation of data provenance, units, assumptions, reproduction instructions, licensing, and file checksums. The release corresponds to six main-text figures, 16 supplementary figures, and 24 supplementary tables. The exact associated manuscript and supplementary document versions are identified by their SHA-256 fingerprints. Data sources include ACEA, FAOSTAT, CWASI, GCAM scenario outputs, USGS irrigation water-use estimates, Kansas irrigation-technology replication data, and complementary water-account datasets. Source-specific citations and attribution requirements are retained in the documentation. Reproduction and validation The documented workflow uses Python 3.11. Separate dependency environments are specified where required. Installing dependencies requires internet access; the numerical analyses use the deposited inputs. Instructions cover the complete workflow and targeted reproduction checks. For version 1.0.1, file checksums, database integrity, and embedded assets were verified. The full-routing analysis was rerun from the deposited GCAM inputs for all 50 future configurations, reproducing the archived global water bounds and joint conservation outcomes within numerical tolerance. This targeted validation does not constitute a new execution of every stage of the study. Interpretation and reuse The modeled water bounds are conditional on specified technology responses, market quantities, supplier availability, production constraints, and water-use coefficients. They are not confidence intervals or globally identified causal effects of irrigation-technology adoption. Future configurations are conditional stress tests, not probabilistic forecasts. Original data compilations and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0, and original analysis code under the MIT License. Third-party inputs retain their source-specific licenses and attribution requirements, as documented in the README. Please cite this repository and the relevant original data sources when reusing the materials.
items.title: Data and code for "Supplier identity can reverse estimates of global irrigation savings"

items.summary: This repository contains the replication data and R code accompanying the study “From Periodic VAT Listings to Real-Time Reporting: Digital Reporting Requirements, Business Information Architecture and the EU VAT Compliance Gap”. The replication package combines European Commission VAT compliance gap data with a manually verified longitudinal coding of mandatory Digital Reporting Requirements across 26 European Union Member States over 2013–2023. The analytical panel contains 284 country-year observations. The policy coding harmonises periodic VAT listings and control statements, SAF-T and invoice-data reporting systems, and continuous or near-real-time transaction controls within a common information-governance framework. Alternative coding scenarios are retained to document uncertainty associated with implementation dates, phased rollouts and differences in reporting architecture. The accompanying R scripts reproduce the analytical dataset construction, descriptive statistics, two-way fixed-effects models, country-specific trend specifications, first-difference analysis, alternative treatment codings, architecture comparisons, panel diagnostics, staggered-adoption diagnostics and wild-cluster bootstrap inference reported in the study. No pre-computed analytical results are included in the repository. All derived results can be reproduced from the supplied input workbook and R scripts. The underlying VAT compliance gap data originate from the European Commission, Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union. The original DRR coding and its documentation were compiled by the authors from official European Commission and national tax-administration sources. The authors’ original data compilation and policy coding are made available under CC BY 4.0. The R replication code is released under the MIT License. Underlying third-party data remain subject to the terms of their original providers.
items.title: Replication Data and R Code for "From Periodic VAT Listings to Real-Time Reporting: Digital Reporting Requirements and the EU VAT Compliance Gap"

items.summary: Analysis code and computed evidence store for the manuscript "An exact recurrence test for acquisition-chain bounds in vehicle telemetry: the closed ECU surface yields nothing, and the one detection lies in the logger we built ourselves", submitted to Sensors and Actuators A: Physical. This deposit contains code and derived results only. The underlying telemetry is published separately under its own DOIs, which fetch_data.py downloads and checksum-verifies before analysis, so the published figures are reproducible from the public record. Study design: observational audit of already-deposited telemetry (seven recording sessions). No experimental control, no intervention, no independent replication, and no statistical power for population-level inference. Headlines formulated after measurement rather than pre-declared in config.json are labelled exploratory in the manuscript. Multiplicity: this deposit is one of 15 analyses drawn from the same corpus of seven sessions, one vehicle and one rider. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied across that family, so the family-wise error rate is not controlled. Repository commit of record: 37f7b2147b26
items.title: Reproducibility package (I-21): An exact recurrence test for acquisition-chain bounds in vehicle telemetry: the closed ECU surface yields nothing, and the one detection lies in the logger we built ourselves

items.summary: We have presented a mathematically closed, comprehensive foundation for the C861 discrete spectral benchmark. By establishing the exact rank-two projector geometry, resolving Dirichlet sum cancellations, providing constructive proofs for linear B-spline KAN operator reproduction, and formalizing the Lyapunov convergence of Dense Associative Memory on spherical manifolds, this framework eliminates ambiguities in evaluating learned physical operators. Furthermore, the spectral interlacing analysis of the CN → PN structural homotopy equips the scientific machine learning community with a tool to distinguish authentic topological sensitivity from numerical discretization artifacts.
items.title: Exact Discrete Spectral Invariants as a Falsification Baseline for Learned Operator

items.summary: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.
items.title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction

items.summary: Weight-space learning across architectures requires representations that respect parameter symmetries and scale to large networks. Existing equivariant tensor encoders require architecture-specific symmetry specifications, while neuron graphs make global attention costly. We introduce a typed graph organized around shared coordinate-permutation actions. Its nodes, called interfaces, represent coordinate spaces whose bound tensor axes must be permuted jointly; operation occurrences, called modules, form typed hyperedges. A compiler derives this graph from supported PyTorch models, with exact recovery of the permutation factors defined by its constraints. The Universal Weight Encoder (UWE) combines local equivariant updates to parameter features with global attention over invariant interface summaries. The small number of interfaces makes global attention practical, and a single encoder processes different supported architectures. UWE is competitive with architecture-specific state-of-the-art methods on established benchmarks. On a new zoo of 1,200 transformers spanning 100 architectures, it outperforms the evaluated baselines at ranking networks within unseen architectures, including architectures larger than those used for training, while using substantially less memory.
items.title: Interfaces and Modules: A Scalable Representation for Weight-Space Learning across Architectures

items.summary: Long-horizon robotic manipulation is often built by chaining independently trained skills. Although each skill can be reliable in isolation, performance degrades sharply when skills are chained: each downstream skill must start from the state its predecessor leaves behind rather than from its training distribution. We study this failure mode, Observation-Space Shift (OSS), and ask what causes these skill-seam failures. Using privileged simulator resets, we find that the dominant shift comes from displaced scene state (e.g., an open drawer or secondary objects left behind by earlier skills), not from the robot's joint configuration or the object the downstream skill manipulates. To test this diagnosis, we build a fully learned detect-restore-resume system: a task-progress monitor detects the stall, a learned policy restores the displaced scene components, and seam-robust fine-tuning lets the skill resume. It recovers the seam where every tested alternative fails, which we treat as evidence for the diagnosis rather than as a general-purpose method. On the BOSS-44 benchmark, the system improves full-chain success from 7.6% to 26.5%, a 3.5x improvement over the base policy and 51% of a privileged restoration oracle, whereas best-of-K resampling, a Diffusion Policy, and world-model baselines fail to recover from the evaluated seam states. On a real Franka arm running a fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ policy, the same monitor is limited by exterior-camera observability, yet closing the loop still recovers some otherwise-terminal failures, motivating wrist and gripper sensing. These results suggest that some long-horizon composition failures are better addressed by restoring the scene before resuming the policy than by retrying from an off-support state.
items.title: Diagnosing and Recovering from Observation-Space Shift at Long-Horizon Skill Seams
